What the original study did not say

The 10,000-hour rule

A popular book turned an average from a study of violinists into a rule.

In 1993, Anders Ericsson and colleagues studied violinists at a Berlin music academy. The best had built up, on average, about 10,000 hours of deliberate practice by the age of 20, more than the good and average players.

Neither a rule nor a magic number

In 2008, Malcolm Gladwell's book Outliers popularised the "10,000-hour rule" as the road to mastery. Ericsson objected: it was an average, many of the best had fewer hours, and what mattered was not quantity but deliberate practice, with specific goals, feedback and effort on what is not yet working.

A 2014 meta-analysis found that practice explains a sizeable share of performance in games and music, but far less in sports or professions. Starting age, motivation, teaching and individual abilities also count.

References

  1. Ericsson, K. A., Krampe, R. T. y Tesch-Römer, C. (1993). The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychological Review, 100(3), 363–406.
  2. Macnamara, B. N., Hambrick, D. Z. y Oswald, F. L. (2014). Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions. Psychological Science, 25(8), 1608–1618.
